part: Part I: Foundations of Data Systems
title: Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Applications
summary: Introduces the three concerns that shape every data system — reliability, scalability, and maintainability — and the vocabulary (faults vs failures, load parameters, response-time percentiles, operability/simplicity/evolvability) for reasoning about them.
keyTakeaways: Data-intensive applications are built by composing standard building blocks — databases, caches, search indexes, stream processing, batch processing — each solving a different need.

Reliability means continuing to work correctly even when things go wrong; a fault is one component deviating from spec, a failure is the whole system stopping service, and fault-tolerance means preventing faults from becoming failures.
Hardware faults are largely random and independent (mitigated by redundancy), while software errors are systematic and correlated across nodes; human error causes most outages.
Scalability is describing load with load parameters and asking what happens to performance as load grows, and what resources you must add to hold performance steady.
Response time should be described with percentiles (p50/p95/p99/p999 tail latencies), not the mean, because tail latency reflects the worst user experiences.
Maintainability rests on operability (easy for ops), simplicity (managing complexity via good abstractions), and evolvability (making change easy).

questions.q: In DDIA's terms, what distinguishes a `fault` from a `failure`?
options: A fault is a bug in application code; a failure is a hardware defect
A fault is recoverable; a failure is permanent and unrecoverable by definition
A fault affects a single user's request; a failure affects all users simultaneously
A fault is one component deviating from its spec; a failure is the system as a whole stopping to provide the required service to users
questions.explain: DDIA defines a fault as one component deviating from spec, and a failure as the whole system stopping service to users. Fault-tolerance is about preventing faults from cascading into failures — the distinction is component-level vs system-level, not hardware-vs-software or recoverable-vs-permanent.

questions.q: Why does DDIA describe hardware faults as easier to reason about than software errors?
options: Hardware faults never cause outages because redundancy always masks them
Hardware faults tend to be random and independent across machines, whereas software errors are systematic and often correlated across many nodes at once
Hardware faults are always detected instantly, while software errors are silent
Software errors can be fixed by rebooting, but hardware faults cannot
questions.explain: Hardware faults (disk crash, RAM fault, power loss) are mostly random and independent, so redundancy like RAID and dual power supplies helps. Software errors are systematic bugs correlated across nodes — a bad input or leap-second bug can take down every replica at once, which redundancy does not protect against.

questions.q: According to DDIA, what is the leading cause of outages, and which mitigation matches it?
options: Disk failures — mitigated by RAID and off-site backups
Network partitions — mitigated by multi-region deployment
Human errors (operator/config mistakes) — mitigated by good abstractions, sandboxes, thorough testing, quick rollback, and telemetry
Memory leaks — mitigated by automatic garbage collection
questions.explain: DDIA cites studies finding humans (configuration errors by operators) as the leading cause of outages. Mitigations target the human loop: well-designed abstractions and APIs, sandbox environments, comprehensive testing, fast rollback of config changes, and detailed telemetry to catch problems early.

questions.q: What is the purpose of deliberately inducing faults in production, as with Netflix's `Chaos Monkey`?
options: To continuously exercise and validate the fault-tolerance machinery so that it works when a real fault occurs, rather than staying untested
To reduce cloud costs by shutting down idle machines
To measure raw throughput under peak load
To force developers to write more unit tests
questions.explain: Fault-tolerance code that is never triggered may be broken when you finally need it. Deliberately injecting faults (killing random processes) keeps the recovery paths continuously exercised, increasing confidence that the system tolerates real faults. It is not a cost or throughput optimization.

questions.q: In DDIA, `scalability` is best described as…
options: The maximum number of servers a system can run on
A property a system either has or lacks, determined by its programming language
A system's ability to cope with increased load, discussed by defining load parameters and asking how performance changes as load grows
The guarantee that response time stays constant no matter how much data is stored
questions.explain: Scalability is not a one-dimensional label ('X is scalable'); it is the ability to cope with increased load, reasoned about by first choosing load parameters, then asking what happens to performance when load grows and what resources are needed to hold performance steady.

questions.q: In the Twitter home-timeline example, what is the `fan-out on write` approach and its main tradeoff?
options: Timelines are computed by querying all followees' tweets at read time, making writes cheap but reads expensive
Tweets are stored only once and never copied, minimizing both read and write cost
Followers poll a central queue on a fixed schedule, decoupling read and write entirely
Each new tweet is inserted into a precomputed cache for every follower at post time, making reads fast but writes costly — especially for users with millions of followers
questions.explain: Fan-out on write pushes each tweet into a cache for every follower when it is posted, so reads are cheap lookups but writes are expensive and amplified by follower count. The read-time alternative (fan-out on read) is cheap to write but expensive to read; Twitter uses a hybrid, fanning out most users on write while handling celebrity accounts on read.

questions.q: DDIA distinguishes `response time` from `latency`. Which statement is correct?
options: They are synonyms and can be used interchangeably
Response time is the duration a request waits before being handled; latency is the total time the client observes
Response time is what the client sees (service time plus network delays plus queueing); latency is the duration a request waits to be serviced
Latency is measured on the server; response time is measured only on the client's CPU
questions.explain: DDIA defines response time as what the client sees — service time plus network and queueing delays — while latency is the duration a request spends waiting to be serviced. The two are related but not identical; conflating them obscures where time is actually spent.

questions.q: Why does DDIA recommend percentiles (e.g. p95, p99) over the arithmetic mean for reporting response times?
options: The mean is harder to compute than percentiles
Percentiles are always smaller than the mean, making the numbers look better
The mean cannot be computed for skewed distributions
The mean does not reveal how many users experience slow responses; percentiles (especially tail latencies) show the worst-case experiences that the mean hides
questions.explain: The mean tells you nothing about how many users hit slow responses and is easily skewed by outliers in both directions. Percentiles — p50 as the typical case, p95/p99/p999 as tail latencies — directly express the experience of the slowest requests, which often correspond to your most valuable, data-heavy customers.

options: A caching technique that reduces the p99 by precomputing results
When a single user request fans out to many backend calls and must wait for the slowest one, so the end-to-end request is slow if any backend call is slow
The tendency of median latency to grow faster than mean latency under load
A monitoring artifact where percentiles are overcounted at high throughput
questions.explain: When one front-end request depends on multiple backend calls, it completes only when the slowest backend responds. As the number of backend calls grows, the chance that at least one is slow rises, so a larger fraction of end-user requests are slow — the tail is amplified. It is a real problem, not a monitoring artifact.

questions.q: What does DDIA mean by `head-of-line blocking` in the context of response-time measurement?
options: A few slow requests hold up a server's limited processing slots, delaying subsequent (even cheap) requests queued behind them
The first request in a batch always gets priority scheduling
Network packets are reordered so the head of the queue arrives last
The database blocks writes while a read is in progress
questions.explain: With limited parallelism, a small number of slow requests can occupy all processing slots and delay every request queued behind them, even quick ones — so client-observed response time rises. This is why load should be measured client-side, since server-side timing misses queueing delay.

questions.q: DDIA contrasts `scaling up` and `scaling out`. Which description is accurate?
options: Scaling up adds more machines; scaling out buys a bigger machine
Scaling up increases network bandwidth; scaling out increases disk capacity
They are the same technique described with different vocabulary
Scaling up (vertical) means a more powerful single machine; scaling out (horizontal) means distributing load across many smaller machines, often a shared-nothing architecture
questions.explain: Scaling up is vertical — a single, more powerful machine. Scaling out is horizontal — spreading load over many commodity machines, commonly shared-nothing. Good architectures usually mix both; DDIA stresses there is no one-size-fits-all 'magic scaling sauce.'

questions.q: What does DDIA mean by an `elastic` system?
options: A system that automatically adds computing resources when it detects a load increase, rather than being scaled manually
A system whose data model can change shape without downtime
A system that compresses data to fit more into memory
A system that guarantees constant latency regardless of load
questions.explain: An elastic system automatically provisions more resources as load rises (and releases them when it falls). The alternative is manual scaling, where a human analyzes capacity and adds machines. Elasticity is about automatic resource adjustment, not data-model flexibility or latency guarantees.

questions.q: DDIA breaks maintainability into three design principles. Which set is correct?
options: Availability, consistency, partition-tolerance
Durability, isolation, atomicity
Operability, simplicity, and evolvability
Throughput, latency, and capacity
questions.explain: DDIA names operability (make it easy for operations teams to keep the system running), simplicity (manage complexity so new engineers can understand the system), and evolvability (make it easy to change the system for future requirements). The other options describe CAP, ACID, and performance metrics — not maintainability.

questions.q: What is `accidental complexity` as DDIA (drawing on Moseley and Marks) uses the term?
options: Complexity inherent in the problem the software solves, which cannot be removed
Complexity that arises only from the implementation, not from the problem itself, and can be removed with better abstractions
Complexity introduced by hardware faults occurring at random times
The unavoidable overhead of running in a distributed environment
questions.explain: Accidental complexity is not inherent to the problem but stems from the implementation — tangled dependencies, inconsistent naming, hacks. It can be removed with good abstractions, unlike essential complexity, which is intrinsic to what the software must do. Managing complexity is the core of the simplicity principle.

questions.prompt: Your API's p50 is 30 ms but p99 is 900 ms and product wants a '200 ms for 99% of requests' SLO. How do you reason about where that tail comes from and how to attack it?
points: Optimize the tail (p99/p999) specifically, not the mean/p50 — the mean hides the slow requests the SLO targets.
Measure response time client-side to capture queueing/head-of-line blocking that server-side timing misses.
Name likely tail causes: head-of-line blocking under limited parallelism, GC pauses, cold caches, contention on the slowest backend.
Watch for tail-latency amplification — if one user request fans out to many backend calls, the request is only as fast as the slowest call.
The heaviest/most-valuable customers (most data) often live in the tail, so the p99 matters commercially, not just cosmetically.
questions.answer: First I'd stop looking at the mean and drive off the p99/p999 directly, measured client-side so I capture queueing and head-of-line blocking, not just server service time. Then I'd decompose the tail: is one request fanning out to many backends so it inherits the slowest one (tail-latency amplification), or is it GC pauses, cold caches, and head-of-line blocking where a few slow requests hog limited slots? I'd attack whichever dominates — cap fan-out, add parallel hedged requests, or fix contention — because the tail is where our heaviest, most valuable users actually live.

questions.prompt: A service is hitting its capacity ceiling. Walk me through how you'd decide between scaling up (a bigger machine) and scaling out (more machines), and what makes the decision.
points: First define the load parameters that are growing (requests/sec, data volume, fan-out) — scalability is relative to a specific load, not an absolute label.
Scaling up (vertical) is simpler operationally but has a hard ceiling and cost/failure-blast-radius grows nonlinearly.
Scaling out (horizontal, shared-nothing) has no single ceiling and improves fault tolerance but adds distributed-systems complexity (coordination, partitioning, consistency).
Stateless request-serving scales out easily; stateful data scaling out forces partitioning/replication decisions.
Real architectures mix both — there is no one-size-fits-all 'magic scaling sauce'; the right split depends on the workload's specific shape.
questions.answer: I'd start by naming which load parameter is actually growing, because scalability is always relative to a specific load, not a badge a system has. If the workload is stateful and heading past what one box can hold, or I need fault tolerance, I lean toward scaling out shared-nothing — but that buys distributed-systems complexity like partitioning and coordination. If a bigger machine buys me runway cheaply and keeps the system simple, I scale up first, since vertical is operationally simpler until it hits its ceiling. In practice it's a mix tuned to the workload; there's no universal scaling recipe.

questions.prompt: You're designing a social feed. Contrast fan-out-on-write versus fan-out-on-read, and tell me which you'd default to and how you'd handle a user with 30 million followers.
points: Fan-out-on-write precomputes each follower's timeline at post time: cheap reads, expensive/amplified writes proportional to follower count.
Fan-out-on-read assembles the timeline by querying followees at read time: cheap writes, expensive reads.
The right default depends on the read:write ratio — feeds are read-heavy, so fan-out-on-write usually wins for the average user.
A celebrity with millions of followers makes write fan-out explode, so handle those accounts on read (hybrid).
The hybrid (fan-out-on-write for normal users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities) is the pragmatic answer Twitter actually adopted.
questions.answer: Fan-out-on-write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed timeline, so reads are cheap lookups but writes are amplified by follower count; fan-out-on-read does the opposite, querying followees at read time. Since feeds are overwhelmingly read-heavy, I'd default to fan-out-on-write for the typical user. But a 30-million-follower account would make a single post trigger 30 million writes, so I'd special-case celebrities and merge their posts in at read time — the hybrid Twitter converged on.

questions.q: Modern cost discussion treats elasticity as bidirectional. What does `scaling down` buy that scaling up does not?
options: Lower tail latency, because fewer nodes means fewer opportunities for a slow replica
Cost proportional to actual load, because capacity provisioned for a peak is billed even while idle
Stronger consistency, because fewer replicas need to agree
Higher durability, because data is concentrated on fewer, better-maintained machines
questions.explain: Under usage-based pricing, idle provisioned capacity is a direct and continuous cost, so releasing it is a first-class design goal rather than tidiness. The consistency and durability options invert the real relationship — fewer replicas generally weakens both.

questions.q: A team moves from a self-managed database to a managed one. Which tradeoff is the real one?
options: You trade operational control — version timing, tuning knobs, failover behavior — for someone else's operational expertise and on-call rota
You trade durability for availability, since managed services replicate asynchronously by default
You trade query expressiveness, since managed services restrict the query language
You trade cost for performance, since managed services are always slower than self-managed equivalents
questions.explain: The exchange is about who operates the thing and how much of its behavior you can still reach — patch windows, failover timing, and tuning surface all narrow. The other options state properties that vary per product rather than the structural tradeoff of managing versus being managed.

questions.q: Why does separating storage from compute change the scaling conversation, rather than just relocating the data?
options: It removes the need for replication, since object storage is already durable
It makes queries faster, because network access to storage beats local disk
It lets you scale the two independently — add query capacity without moving data, or grow the dataset without adding compute
It guarantees elasticity, because compute nodes become stateless and therefore instantly replaceable
questions.explain: The point is decoupling two resources that used to grow together on the same box, so each can follow its own demand curve. The stateless-compute option is close but overstated — the compute tier still holds caches and in-flight state, so replacement is cheaper, not instant.

questions.q: A service is defining nonfunctional requirements. Which framing makes cost a genuine requirement rather than an afterthought?
options: A total monthly budget ceiling for the service
A cost per unit of work — per request, per user, per GB processed — tracked alongside latency and availability
A commitment to use the cheapest available instance type
An annual review comparing spend against the previous year
questions.explain: Normalizing cost per unit of work makes it comparable across load levels and directly tradeable against latency and availability, which is what a requirement has to be. A total ceiling (the tempting distractor) tells you nothing about whether the system got more or less efficient as it grew.

questions.prompt: Your service is provisioned for a peak that occurs two hours a day. Finance asks why the bill is flat. Explain the tradeoff space and what you'd actually change.
points: Name the cause: capacity is provisioned for peak but billed continuously, so 22 hours a day you are paying for headroom you are not using.
The naive fix — provision for average — fails the peak, so the real question is how fast you can add capacity relative to how fast load arrives.
Autoscaling closes the gap only if the scale-up time is shorter than the ramp; if load spikes faster than nodes boot, you are back to pre-provisioning.
Warm-pool or over-provision-by-a-margin designs sit between the two: pay for a fraction of peak headroom continuously rather than all of it.
Name the counterweight from reliability: static stability argues for pre-provisioned capacity precisely so recovery does not depend on a control plane that may also be degraded.
Land on the framing — this is cost per unit of work versus availability risk, and the right answer depends on the cost of a dropped request during the two-hour peak.
Mention scale-to-zero as the extreme case: viable for spiky, latency-tolerant workloads, disqualifying where cold-start latency is user-visible.
questions.answer: The bill is flat because we provision for peak and pay continuously, so for twenty-two hours a day we're renting headroom we don't use. The naive fix — provision for average — just fails the peak, so the real question is whether we can add capacity faster than load arrives. If the ramp is gradual, autoscaling closes most of the gap; if load spikes faster than nodes boot, we're back to pre-provisioning and the honest answer is that the headroom is the price of the peak. There's also a reliability counterweight: static stability argues for pre-provisioned capacity so recovery doesn't depend on a control plane that might be degraded too. I'd frame the decision as cost per request against the cost of dropping requests during those two hours, and I'd only consider scale-to-zero if cold starts aren't user-visible.
